title: Supply Chain and Logistics Fundamentals
summary: Learn how supply chains work, choose suppliers, manage inventory with EOQ and reorder points, run warehouses, compare transport and Incoterms, and track performance and risk.
audience: Students, procurement and stores staff, small-business owners and anyone moving into logistics

body.p: A supply chain is the network of organisations, people and activities that turns raw materials into products in customers' hands: suppliers, factories, warehouses, transporters, retailers and the customer. Supply chain management (SCM) plans and coordinates all of it so that the right product reaches the right place at the right time, in the right condition, at the right cost.

list: Goods move from suppliers towards customers (and returns move back).
Information moves both ways: forecasts and orders upstream, delivery updates downstream.
Money moves from customers back up the chain as payment.

body.p: Small changes in customer demand can become large swings further up the chain. A shop sees sales rise 5%, orders 10% extra to be safe; the distributor adds its own buffer; the factory sees a jump of 30% and hires extra staff, then demand settles and everyone is overstocked. Sharing real sales data and planning together reduces this effect.

body.tip: Think of the chain as a team: a cheaper supplier that delivers late can cost more in lost sales than it saves.

body.p: Procurement is the process of finding, choosing and buying from suppliers. It covers identifying needs, writing specifications, requesting quotations or tenders, evaluating offers, negotiating, contracting and managing supplier performance. Public bodies must follow strict, transparent procurement rules to prevent corruption.

Score each supplier from 1 to 10 on agreed criteria and weight them by importance. With weights price 40%, quality 35% and delivery reliability 25%: supplier A scores 7, 9 and 8, giving 0.4 x 7 + 0.35 x 9 + 0.25 x 8 = 7.95; supplier B scores 9, 6 and 7, giving 7.45. A is chosen despite its higher price because it is better on quality and delivery.

list: Purchase price is only part of the cost.
Add transport, import duties, storage, quality failures and returns.
Include maintenance, energy use and disposal for equipment.
Consider payment terms: 60 days to pay frees cash compared with paying upfront.

body.tip: Keep at least two approved suppliers for critical items so one failure does not stop your business.

body.p: Inventory is stock held to meet demand: raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. Too little causes stock-outs and lost sales; too much ties up cash, takes space and risks spoilage or obsolescence.

The economic order quantity (EOQ) balances ordering costs against holding costs: EOQ = √(2DS/H), where D is annual demand, S the cost per order and H the cost of holding one unit for a year. With D = 12 000 units, S = R500 and H = R12, EOQ = √(2 x 12 000 x 500 / 12) = 1000 units, so the business orders 12 times a year. At this quantity holding cost (1000/2 x 12 = R6000) equals ordering cost (12 x 500 = R6000).

Reorder point = daily demand x lead time + safety stock. If 40 units are used a day, delivery takes 7 days and safety stock is 100 units, reorder when stock falls to 40 x 7 + 100 = 380 units. Safety stock protects against late deliveries and demand spikes.

Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory value. A shop with R1.2 million cost of sales and R200 000 average stock turns its stock 6 times a year, holding about 365 / 6, roughly 61 days of stock.

body.tip: Use ABC analysis: the few high-value A items deserve tight control and frequent review; the many low-value C items can be managed simply.

body.p: Warehouses receive, store, pick, pack and dispatch goods. A good layout puts fast-moving items near the dispatch area, keeps aisles clear and safe, and labels every location so goods can be found quickly.

list: FIFO (first in, first out): older stock leaves first, good for most goods.
FEFO (first expired, first out): items with the earliest expiry leave first, essential for food and medicines.
LIFO (last in, first out): sometimes used for non-perishable bulk goods such as sand or coal piles.
Record every movement in a stock system, using barcodes or scanners where possible.
Run cycle counts, counting a few locations daily, instead of one disruptive annual count.
Investigate gaps between recorded and physical stock; they reveal theft, damage or recording errors.
Train staff in safe lifting, forklift use and fire safety.

body.p: ABC analysis often finds that about 20% of items make up about 80% of the stock value. Count those A items most often.

body.tip: A cold chain (refrigerated storage and transport) must be monitored continuously for vaccines and fresh food; one warm hour can spoil the whole batch.

body.p: Logistics moves goods efficiently. Each transport mode has trade-offs: road is flexible and door to door; rail is cheaper for heavy bulk over long distances; sea is cheapest per tonne for international trade but slow; air is fast and expensive, used for urgent or high-value goods.

Compare options on cost per tonne or per unit, not per trip. A truck charging R18 000 to carry 30 tonnes costs 18 000 / 30 = R600 a tonne. A part-full truck costs the same, so consolidating loads and planning return trips cuts costs.

list: EXW (Ex Works): the buyer collects from the seller's premises and bears almost all cost and risk.
FOB (Free On Board): the seller loads goods onto the ship; risk passes to the buyer once they are on board.
CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight): the seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port, but risk passes at loading.
DDP (Delivered Duty Paid): the seller delivers to the buyer's door with duties paid, bearing the most cost and risk.

body.p: Cross-border trade also needs correct documents (invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, customs declarations). Agreements such as the African Continental Free Trade Area aim to cut tariffs and border delays between African countries.

body.tip: Always state the Incoterm and named place in contracts, for example "FOB Mombasa".

body.p: Supply chains are managed with key performance indicators (KPIs). Common ones are on-time-in-full (OTIF), fill rate, lead time, inventory turnover, cost per order and forecast accuracy. If 450 of 500 orders arrive on time and complete, OTIF = 450 / 500 = 90%.

list: Map critical suppliers and routes, including your suppliers' suppliers.
Hold safety stock for critical items and consider dual sourcing.
Build relationships and share forecasts with key partners.
Have contingency plans for strikes, port delays, power cuts and extreme weather.

body.p: Customers, investors and regulators increasingly expect firms to cut emissions and waste, avoid child and forced labour, and respect the environment across their supply chains. Practical steps include fuller loads and better routes, reusable packaging, local sourcing where it makes sense, supplier codes of conduct and audits.

body.tip: Measure a few KPIs well and review them regularly; a long list of unmeasured targets changes nothing.
